questions.prompt:
What is wrong with this comparator?
```cpp
std::sort(pts.begin(), pts.end(),
          [](const Pt& a, const Pt& b) { return a.range <= b.range; });
```
options: Nothing, it sorts ascending
Sorts descending
Compile error: comparator must be a function pointer
Violates strict weak ordering: `cmp(a,a)` is true. UB, and `std::sort` can read out of bounds with many equal keys
questions.explanation: Comparators must be **irreflexive**: `cmp(a, a)` must be false. With `<=`, equal elements compare true both ways. libstdc++'s unguarded insertion sort relies on that guarantee and can run past the end of the range, which is a real ASan heap-buffer-overflow when many ranges are equal. Use `<`.

questions.prompt: Which hash is the worst for 2-D grid cells `(x, y)` with small coordinates around the robot?

questions.explanation: With libstdc++, `std::hash<int>` is the identity. Then `x ^ y` maps `(a,b)` and `(b,a)` to the same value, maps every `(k,k)` to 0, and squeezes a 100x100 neighbourhood into 128 distinct values, so buckets degenerate and lookups approach O(n). (B) uses the Teschner spatial-hash primes, (C) is boost's `hash_combine`, and (D) packs both coordinates losslessly into 64 bits.

questions.prompt:
Lazy Dijkstra: why is this check needed?
```cpp
auto [d, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
if (d > dist[u]) continue;   // <-- this line
```
options: `std::priority_queue` has no decrease-key, so outdated duplicate entries for `u` must be skipped
To handle negative edges
To avoid integer overflow
It isn't needed; it is only an optimization for A*
questions.explanation: Rather than updating a key in place, we push a new `(newDist, v)` each time `v` improves, so the heap can hold several entries for one node. The stale ones have `d > dist[u]`. Skipping them keeps the run time at O(E log E). Without the check, the result is still correct for non-negative weights, but you re-relax edges needlessly. Negative edges break Dijkstra either way.

questions.prompt: Top-k closest points out of n = 10⁶, k = 10. Which is the best fit?
options: `std::sort` everything, take the first k: O(n log n)
Bounded max-heap of size k: O(n log k), O(k) memory
A min-heap of all n points, pop k times: O(n log n) to build
`std::set` of all points: O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Keep the k best so far in a **max**-heap, so `top()` is the worst of them, and replace it whenever a closer point appears. That is O(n log k), roughly n × 3.3 comparisons for k = 10, and it streams. `std::nth_element` + sort of the first k (O(n + k log k)) is also excellent when everything fits in memory. Pushing all n points into a min-heap with `make_heap` is O(n + k log n), which is fine but uses O(n) extra memory.
